# Cholera and typhoid spread through drinking water (`cholera_waterborne`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by epidemiology_mapping, contagion_theory, boiled_water, microscope
- Core idea: Cholera, typhoid and dysentery are swallowed: the excrement of the sick gets into wells and rivers and onto hands and food, and swallowing contaminated food or water may cause infection, sometimes without symptoms. Smell does not matter; men working in the sewers were not struck more than others. The proof is Snow's comparison of two London water companies supplying the same streets in 1854: houses served with sewage-tainted Thames water had 315 cholera deaths per 10,000 houses, houses served from above the city had 37. So: close or boil suspect sources, move intakes upstream, keep latrines away from wells, and wash hands after nursing the sick. Fluid loss is the immediate danger. Oral rehydration treats most cases; severe dehydration requires urgent intravenous fluid as well.
- Pitfalls:
  - Telling the pump-handle story as the proof; the outbreak was already fading and the map came later, the water-company comparison is the strong evidence
  - Treating cholera with bleeding, calomel or by withholding water, the usual treatments, which kill
  - Believing clear water from a deep-looking well is safe; the Broad Street well was fouled by a cesspit a metre away
  - Mixing up typhoid (water, food, carriers) with typhus (lice)
  - Expecting Asiatic cholera in Europe before 1830; the word 'cholera' in older texts means ordinary vomiting and diarrhoea
- History: india: 1817 – first pandemic spreads from Bengal, where cholera was long endemic; 1884 Koch identifies the bacterium in Calcutta; europe: 1831 – cholera reaches western Europe; 1849 and 1855 Snow's water theory; 1854 Pacini sees the vibrio in Florence (ignored); 1856–1873 Budd on typhoid; 1892 Hamburg epidemic settles the dispute; americas: 1832 – cholera reaches North America
- Read:
  - John Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera (2nd ed., 1855)
  - Steven Johnson, The Ghost Map (2006)
  - Sandra Hempel, The Medical Detective: John Snow, Cholera and the Mystery of the Broad Street Pump (2006)
